| Column 1 | Column 2 | Column 3 |
|---|---|---|
| i. Triad | c. Average of the first and the third atomic mass | 5. Dobereiner |
| ii. Octave | d. Properties of the eighth element similar to the first | 3. Newlands |
| iii. Atomic number | e. Positive charge on the nucleus | 6. Moseley |
| iv. Period | f. Sequential change in molecular formulae | 1. Mendeleev |
| v. Nucleus | b. Concentrated mass and positive charge | 4. Rutherford |
| vi. Electron | a. Lightest and negatively charged particle in all the atoms | 2. Thomson |

Where each pairing comes from:

- **Triad** — the chapter says that in 1817 Dobereiner "made groups of three elements each, having similar chemical properties and called them triads", and "showed that the atomic mass of the middle element was approximately equal to the mean of the atomic masses of the other two elements". That mean is the average of the first and the third atomic mass.
- **Octave** — Newlands, in 1866, "found that every eighth element had properties similar to those of the first" and "called the similarity observed in the eighth and the first element as the Law of octaves".
- **Atomic number** — in 1913 Moseley "demonstrated, with the help of the experiments done using X-ray tube, that the atomic number (Z) of an element corresponds to the positive charge on the nucleus or the number of the protons in the nucleus".
- **Period** — the chapter says "The vertical columns in the Mendeleev's periodic table are called groups while the horizontal rows are called periods", and the head of every group of that table carries a general molecular formula for the oxide and the hydride \(\left(\mathrm{R_{2}O},\ \mathrm{RO},\ \mathrm{R_{2}O_{3}},\ \mathrm{RO_{2}},\ \mathrm{R_{2}O_{5}},\ \mathrm{RO_{3}},\ \mathrm{R_{2}O_{7}},\ \mathrm{RO_{4}}\right)\), so those formulae change sequentially as one reads across a period.
- **Nucleus** and **Electron** — this chapter does not mention Rutherford or Thomson anywhere in its own text; the two names occur only in this exercise's own Column 3. The pairings are the ones left over, and they rest on work done in an earlier standard: Thomson discovered the electron, the lightest negatively charged particle present in all atoms, and Rutherford discovered the nucleus, in which the atom's mass and positive charge are concentrated.

The atomic number is **12**.

The configuration 2,8,2 accounts for \(2+8+2=12\) electrons, and the chapter states that "the total number of electrons in an atom is same as the atomic number". The element is therefore magnesium — table 2.7 gives Mg the configuration 2,8,2.

It belongs to **group 2**.

The outermost shell of this element holds 2 electrons, and the chapter says the number of valence electrons is what fixes the group: "the elements beryllium (Be), magnesium (Mg) and calcium (Ca) belong to the group 2, that is, the family of alkaline earth metals. There are two electrons in their outermost shell."

It belongs to the **third period**.

Its electrons occupy three shells (K, L and M). The chapter says "the elements with the same number of shells occupied by electrons belong to the same period", and names the third period as "Na, Mg, Al, Si, P, S, Cl and Ar", which "have electrons in the three shells; K, L and M".

It resembles **Be (4)**, beryllium.

The configurations of the four candidates are N (7) = 2,5 · Be (4) = 2,2 · Ar (18) = 2,8,8 · Cl (17) = 2,8,7. Only beryllium has two electrons in its outermost shell, the same as the given element (2,8,2), so the two lie in the same group. The chapter states that "the electronic configuration of the outermost shell is characteristic of a particular group" and that "Various properties of all the elements in a group show similarity and gradation".

Electronic configurations: Li (3) = 2,1 · Si (14) = 2,8,4 · He (2) = 2 · Na (11) = 2,8,1 · P (15) = 2,8,5.

**Silicon, sodium and phosphorus** belong to the third period.

Explanation: the chapter says "the elements with the same number of shells occupied by electrons belong to the same period", and names the third period as "Na, Mg, Al, Si, P, S, Cl and Ar". Silicon, sodium and phosphorus each have electrons in three shells. Lithium has electrons in two shells and so lies in the second period, and helium has electrons in one shell only and lies in the first period.

Electronic configurations: H (1) = 1 · N (7) = 2,5 · Ca (20) = 2,8,8,2 · S (16) = 2,8,6 · Be (4) = 2,2 · Ar (18) = 2,8,8.

**Calcium and beryllium** belong to the second group.

Explanation: the chapter says that within a group "the number of their valence electrons" is the same, and that group 2 is "the family of alkaline earth metals" whose members beryllium (Be), magnesium (Mg) and calcium (Ca) have "two electrons in their outermost shell". Calcium (2,8,8,2) and beryllium (2,2) are the two here with two valence electrons. Hydrogen has one, nitrogen five, sulphur six and argon eight.

[Textbook note: the book prints the fifth symbol as A1 — a capital A followed by the digit one — but atomic number 13 is aluminium, whose symbol is Al. The same page prints C1 for Cl in item (e), and printed p21 of this chapter prints both Cl and C1 for chlorine in a single sentence, so this is a typesetting fault rather than a different element. Answered as aluminium.]

Electronic configurations: N (7) = 2,5 · C (6) = 2,4 · O (8) = 2,6 · B (5) = 2,3 · Al (13) = 2,8,3.

The most electronegative element among these is **oxygen (O)**.

Explanation: boron, carbon, nitrogen and oxygen all lie in the second period, and the chapter states that electronegativity goes on increasing from left to right within a period — "Due to increasing electronegativity from left to right within a period, the ability of an atom to become anion by accepting outside electrons goes on increasing." Of these four, oxygen lies farthest to the right, so it is the most electronegative. Aluminium is a metal of the third period, on the left of the zig-zag line, and is electropositive rather than electronegative.

[Textbook note: the book prints the fifth symbol as A1 — a capital A followed by the digit one — but atomic number 13 is aluminium, whose symbol is Al. See the note on item (c). Answered as aluminium.]

Electronic configurations: Be (4) = 2,2 · C (6) = 2,4 · O (8) = 2,6 · B (5) = 2,3 · Al (13) = 2,8,3.

The most electropositive element among these is **aluminium (Al)**.

Explanation: the chapter says that metal atoms "have a tendency to form a cation by losing its valence electron, this property is called electropositivity of an element". Of these five only beryllium and aluminium are metals — boron lies on the zig-zag line as a metalloid, and carbon and oxygen lie to its right as nonmetals. Between the two metals, aluminium's valence electrons are in the third shell while beryllium's are in the second. The chapter's own mechanism settles the comparison: "while going down a group a new shell gets added, resulting in an increase in the distance between the nucleus and the valence electrons. This results in lowering the effective nuclear charge and thereby lowering the attractive force on the valence electrons. As a result of this the tendency of the atom to lose electrons increases." The outer electrons of aluminium are farther from the nucleus and better screened by the inner shells, so it loses them more readily than beryllium does.

(The chapter states the group trend and the period trend separately and gives no single rule for comparing two elements that differ in both; the comparison above rests on the shell-distance mechanism it does state.)

[Textbook note: the book prints the third symbol as C1 — a capital C followed by the digit one — but atomic number 17 is chlorine, whose symbol is Cl. Printed p21 of this chapter prints both Cl and C1 for chlorine in a single sentence, and printed p19 prints the two chlorine isotopes as C1-35 and C1-37, so this is a typesetting fault rather than a different element. Answered as chlorine.]

Electronic configurations: Na (11) = 2,8,1 · P (15) = 2,8,5 · Cl (17) = 2,8,7 · Si (14) = 2,8,4 · Mg (12) = 2,8,2.

**Sodium (Na)** has the largest atoms.

Explanation: all five have electrons in three shells, so all five lie in the third period. The chapter states that "atomic radius goes on decreasing while going from left to right within a period", because the nuclear charge rises one unit at a time while the extra electron enters the same outermost shell. Sodium is the leftmost of the five, in group 1, so its atoms are the largest. The chapter's own data agrees: it gives sodium an atomic radius of 186 pm.

Electronic configurations: K (19) = 2,8,8,1 · Li (3) = 2,1 · Na (11) = 2,8,1 · Be (4) = 2,2.

**Beryllium (Be)** has the smallest atomic radius.

Explanation: potassium, sodium and lithium are all group 1 elements with four, three and two occupied shells respectively, and the chapter says "while going down a group the atomic size goes on increasing", so lithium is the smallest of those three. Beryllium lies in the same period as lithium but one place to its right, and "atomic radius goes on decreasing while going from left to right within a period", so beryllium is smaller still. The chapter's two printed radius tables confirm it directly: Be 111 pm, Li 152 pm, Na 186 pm, K 231 pm.

[Textbook note: the book prints the first symbol as A1 — a capital A followed by the digit one — but atomic number 13 is aluminium, whose symbol is Al. See the note on item (c). Answered as aluminium.]

Electronic configurations: Al (13) = 2,8,3 · Si (14) = 2,8,4 · Na (11) = 2,8,1 · Mg (12) = 2,8,2 · S (16) = 2,8,6.

**Sodium (Na)** has the highest metallic character.

Explanation: all five have electrons in three shells and so lie in the third period. The chapter says "The metallic character of an atom is its tendency to lose electrons", and that within a period "the positive charge on the nucleus goes on increasing while the atomic radius goes on decreasing and thus the effective nuclear charge goes on increasing. As a result of this the tendency of atom to lose valence electrons decreases within a period from left to right." Sodium is the leftmost of the five, in group 1 with a single valence electron, so it loses that electron most readily. The chapter also names sodium and magnesium as "the metallic elements" lying towards the left of the third period.

Electronic configurations: C (6) = 2,4 · Li (3) = 2,1 · F (9) = 2,7 · N (7) = 2,5 · O (8) = 2,6.

**Fluorine (F)** has the highest nonmetallic character.

Explanation: all five have electrons in two shells and so lie in the second period. The chapter says "The tendency of an element to form anion or the electro negativity is the nonmetallic character of an element", and that electronegativity goes on increasing from left to right within a period. Fluorine lies farthest to the right of the five, with seven valence electrons and so needing only one more to complete its octet, so its nonmetallic character is the highest.

**Helium, He.**

The chapter gives two trends in atomic size: "atomic radius goes on decreasing while going from left to right within a period" and "while going down a group the atomic size goes on increasing". Taken together, the smallest atom is the one lying at the top right of the periodic table. In table 2.7 the first period holds only hydrogen and helium, and helium is the right-hand of the two, so helium has the smallest atom.

(The chapter tabulates no atomic radius for hydrogen or for helium — the smallest value it prints is 66 pm for oxygen — so this answer follows from the two trends the chapter states rather than from a printed number.)

**Hydrogen, H.**

The chapter states, of the arrangement of elements in an increasing order of their atomic masses, that "It started with the lightest element hydrogen and ended up with thorium". Table 2.7 also gives hydrogen the smallest atomic mass of all the elements, 1.008.

**Fluorine, F.**

The chapter states that electronegativity increases from left to right within a period, and its "Always remember" box states that "While going downwards in any group the electropositivity of elements goes on increasing while their electronegativity goes on decreasing." So the most electronegative atom lies at the top right of the table. The noble gases of group 18 are set aside, because the chapter defines electronegativity as the tendency of an atom "to become anion by accepting outside electrons", and a noble gas already has the stable configuration that such ions attain. That leaves fluorine, the topmost member of the halogen family in group 17.

(The chapter does not name fluorine as the most electronegative element in so many words; the answer follows from the two trends it states.)

**Helium, He.**

The noble gases occupy group 18 of the modern periodic table, and the chapter states that "while going down a group the atomic size goes on increasing. This is because while going down a group a new shell is added. Therefore the distance between the outermost electron and the nucleus goes on increasing." Helium is the topmost member of group 18 in table 2.7, with electrons in a single shell, so of all the noble gases its atomic radius is the smallest.

**Fluorine, F.**

The chapter's "Always remember" box states that "Larger the electropositivity or electronegativity of the element higher the reactivity." Fluorine is the most electronegative element (see the answer to Q.5 c), so among the nonmetals it is the most reactive.

Mendeleev's periodic law states:

> "Properties of elements are periodic function of their atomic masses."

How he arrived at it, as the chapter describes: Dmitri Mendeleev, a Russian scientist and a professor at the St. Petersburg University, developed his periodic table during the period 1869 to 1872 A.D. He took "the fundamental property of elements, namely, the atomic mass, as standard" and arranged the 63 elements known at that time in an increasing order of their atomic masses. He then organised that arrangement into a table on the basis of the physical and chemical properties of the elements — "the molecular formulae of hydrides and oxides of the elements, melting points, boiling points and densities of the elements and their hydrides and oxides". He found "that the elements with similar physical and chemical properties repeat after a definite interval", and the periodic law above is the statement of that finding.

In the table he built on this law the vertical columns are called groups and the horizontal rows are called periods.

Structure of the modern periodic table, as the chapter sets it out:

- The elements are arranged in an increasing order of their **atomic numbers**, following the modern periodic law that "Properties of elements are a periodic function of their atomic numbers." It is also called the **long form** of the periodic table.
- It contains **seven horizontal rows called the periods**, 1 to 7.
- It contains **eighteen vertical columns called the groups**, 1 to 18.
- Periods and groups together form boxes, one box for each element, with the atomic numbers indicated serially in the upper part of the boxes.
- Two further rows are shown separately at the bottom — the **lanthanide series** and the **actinide series**.
- Including these two series there are **118 boxes**, that is, 118 places for elements; all 118 elements are now discovered, so the table is completely filled.
- The table is divided into **four blocks**: the s-block is groups 1 and 2; the p-block is groups 13 to 18; the d-block is groups 3 to 12, whose elements are called transition elements; and the lanthanide and actinide series at the bottom form the f-block.
- A **zig-zag line** can be drawn in the p-block. "All the metals lie on the left side of the zig-zag line while all the nonmetals lie on the right side", and "The metalloid elements lie along the border of this zig-zag line."
- Elements of the same group show similarity and gradation in their properties, while along a period the properties change slowly from one end to the other.

**In Mendeleev's periodic table.** That table was built on atomic mass — "Properties of elements are periodic function of their atomic masses" — so two isotopes of one element, having different atomic masses, should occupy different places in it. But their chemical properties are identical, which requires them to occupy the same place. The chapter records this among the demerits of the table: "Isotopes were discovered long time after Mendeleev put forth the periodic table. As isotopes have the same chemical properties but different atomic masses, a challenge was posed in placing them in Mendeleev's periodic table." No separate places were in fact given to isotopes; the two isotopes of chlorine, of atomic masses 35 and 37, were placed together in the single box for chlorine, which the periodic law as stated could not justify.

**In the modern periodic table.** That table is built on atomic number — "Properties of elements are a periodic function of their atomic numbers" — and the isotopes of an element all have the same atomic number, since Moseley showed the atomic number to be "the positive charge on the nucleus or the number of the protons in the nucleus", which is the same for every isotope of an element. So all the isotopes of an element occupy one and the same place, and no difficulty arises. Both isotopes of chlorine are placed in the box for atomic number 17.

(This chapter does not define what an isotope is — that was done in an earlier standard — and it poses the placement of the chlorine isotopes as a question in its "Think about it" and "Use your brain power" boxes rather than answering it in prose.)

Within a period, the number of shells occupied by electrons stays the same while the atomic number rises one unit at a time. The chapter gives the reason in these words:

> "While going from left to right within a period, the atomic number increases one by one, meaning the positive charge on the nucleus increases by one unit at a time. However, the additional electron gets added to the same outermost shell. Due to the increased nuclear charge the electrons are pulled towards the nucleus to a greater extent and thereby the size of the atom decreases."

So the growing positive charge on the nucleus pulls the same outermost shell inwards, and since atomic radius is "the distance between the nucleus of the atom and its outermost shell", that radius goes on decreasing from left to right in a period.

The chapter defines the metallic character of an atom as "its tendency to lose electrons", which it also calls electropositivity.

Across a period the outermost shell remains the same, while, in the chapter's words:

> "the positive charge on the nucleus goes on increasing while the atomic radius goes on decreasing and thus the effective nuclear charge goes on increasing. As a result of this the tendency of atom to lose valence electrons decreases within a period from left to right."

Because the valence electrons are held with a greater and greater attractive force, the atom parts with them less and less readily — so the metallic character goes on decreasing from left to right in a period. (The same two factors raise the electronegativity, which is why the nonmetallic character rises in that direction.)

The chapter gives the reason in these words:

> "while going down a group the atomic size goes on increasing. This is because while going down a group a new shell is added. Therefore the distance between the outermost electron and the nucleus goes on increasing. As a result of this the atomic size increases in spite of the increased nuclear charge."

So although the nuclear charge also rises down a group, the addition of a whole new shell at each step moves the outermost electrons farther out, and that effect dominates. Since atomic radius is "the distance between the nucleus of the atom and its outermost shell", the atomic radius goes on increasing down a group. The chapter's own data shows it: Li 152 pm, Na 186 pm, K 231 pm, Rb 244 pm, Cs 262 pm.

The chapter states that "the valency of an element is determined by the number of electrons present in the outermost shell of its atoms, that is, the valence electrons".

It also states that the number of valence electrons is fixed for a group: "the number of valence electrons in all these elements from the group 1, that is, the family of alkali metals, is the same. Similarly, if you look at the elements from any other group, you will find the number of their valence electrons to be the same" — and hence "the electronic configuration of the outermost shell is characteristic of a particular group".

Since valency depends only on the number of valence electrons, and that number is the same for every element of a group, all the elements belonging to a group have the same valency. For example, in group 1 the configurations are Li 2,1 · Na 2,8,1 · K 2,8,8,1 — one valence electron each, so the valency of each is 1.

The electron capacity of a shell is \(2n^{2}\), where n is the shell number. For the M shell \(n=3\), so its capacity is \(2\times 3^{2}=18\) electrons, as table 2.9 of the chapter shows.

The number of elements in a period is nevertheless fixed by how many electrons are actually filled into the outermost shell before a new shell begins. The chapter states:

> "As per the electron holding capacity of shells 2 elements are present in the first period and 8 elements in the second period. The third period also contains only eight elements due to the law of electron octet."

Once the outermost shell has received eight electrons it is a complete octet and is stable, so filling of the M shell stops at eight; the ninth electron opens a new shell and with it a new period. Argon, 2,8,8, is therefore the last element of the third period even though its M shell is not yet full. (The chapter adds that "There are few more factors which control the filling of electrons in the subsequent periods which will be considered in the next standards.")

**The third period.**

The chapter states: "The elements in the third period, namely, Na, Mg, Al, Si, P, S, Cl and Ar have electrons in the three shells; K, L and M."

**Group 18** — the family of noble gases, which the chapter also calls the inert gases.

The atoms of this group have a complete outermost shell: table 2.8 gives helium 2, neon 2,8 and argon 2,8,8. They therefore neither lose nor gain electrons to form ions — the chapter notes that ions of other elements attain "a stable electronic configuration of a noble gas", which these atoms already possess — so their valency is zero.

(The chapter does not print the phrase "valency zero"; it asks the reader to work out the valency trend "with reference to the group 1, group 2 and group 18", and the answer above is what that exercise yields.)

**The halogen family**, that is, group 17.

The chapter states: "there are seven electrons in the outermost shell of the elements such as fluorine (F) and chlorine (Cl) from the group 17, that is, the family of halogens", and "The group 17 contains the members of the halogen family." With seven valence electrons an atom needs one more to complete its octet, so the valency of these nonmetals is \(8-7=1\).

**The alkali metals**, that is, group 1.

The chapter calls group 1 "the family of alkali metals" and says the number of valence electrons is the same throughout it. Table 2.8 gives Li 2,1 · Na 2,8,1 · K 2,8,8,1 — one valence electron each — and since valency is fixed by the number of valence electrons, each of these metals has valency 1.

**The alkaline earth metals**, that is, group 2.

The chapter states: "the elements beryllium (Be), magnesium (Mg) and calcium (Ca) belong to the group 2, that is, the family of alkaline earth metals. There are two electrons in their outermost shell." Two valence electrons give a valency of 2.

**Boron (B)** in the second period and **silicon (Si)** in the third period.

The chapter states that a zig-zag line can be drawn in the p-block of the modern periodic table, that "All the metals lie on the left side of the zig-zag line while all the nonmetals lie on the right side", and that "The metalloid elements lie along the border of this zig-zag line." It names the third period's metalloid outright: "The metalloid element silicon lies in between these two types." In table 2.7 the zig-zag line runs along the lower edge of the boron box and then down the right-hand side of aluminium, so boron is the second-period element sitting on that border.

(The chapter names only silicon as a metalloid in its prose; boron is read off the zig-zag line drawn in table 2.7, using the rule quoted above.)

**Phosphorus (P), sulphur (S) and chlorine (Cl).**

The third period runs Na, Mg, Al, Si, P, S, Cl, Ar. The chapter classifies it as follows: "It is seen that the metallic elements like sodium, magnesium are towards the left. The nonmetallic elements such as sulphur, chlorine are towards the right. The metalloid element silicon lies in between these two types." So sodium, magnesium and aluminium are the metals, silicon is the metalloid, and phosphorus, sulphur and chlorine are the nonmetals.

Argon, the last element of the period, also lies to the right of the zig-zag line and is a nonmetal, but it is the period's noble gas — the chapter treats the noble gases as a family of their own.

**Carbon (C) and silicon (Si).**

Table 2.8 of the chapter gives carbon the configuration 2,4 and silicon the configuration 2,8,4, so each has four electrons in its outermost shell. Since "the valency of an element is determined by the number of electrons present in the outermost shell of its atoms", the valency of each is 4. They are the second-period and third-period members of the same group, group 14.
